title: Email change
description: Letting a signed-in user move the account to a new address, with fresh authentication, a code to the new address, a revert link to the old one, and what the routes must do with each answer.
---

import { Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import routesTs from '../../../../snippets/build/email-change/routes.ts?raw';

The core has four flows for changing the account's email: `requestEmailChange`, `confirmEmailChangeCode` (or `confirmEmailChangeLink`), and `revertEmailChange`. Why each rule is there is in [Email change](/auth/learn/email-change/). This guide builds on [A Node server with Redis and Prisma](/auth/build/node-server/).

## What it needs

- **A user store with `changeEmail`.** `PrismaUserStore` and `MemoryUserStore` have it. The method is optional on the `UserStore` port so older adapters still compile, and the email change flows throw an `AuthConfigError` without it. A store of your own must keep the email column unique and pass the `changeEmail` cases of `userStoreConformance` (see [Writing a store adapter](/auth/build/store-adapter/)).
- **`urls.revertEmailChange`.** The link mailed to the old address. The flows throw an `AuthConfigError` without it. Put the token in the fragment, as the node-server sample does, and send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
- **Templates** for four mail events: `email-change-confirm`, `email-change-in-use`, `email-changed` and `email-change-reverted` ([Mail](/auth/build/mail/)).

No new table: the code, the revert link, the hold on the old address and the block after a revert are rows of the one-time token table you already have, under their own purposes. The hold is filed under a key derived from the address (`email-reserved:` and its SHA-256) instead of a user id, so a token store must not assume that column names a user.

## The routes

<Code code={routesTs} lang="ts" title="src/routes/email.ts" />

**Request.** The session must be live and its last credential proof younger than `session.freshAuthAge` (10 minutes by default), or the answer is `fresh_auth_required`: send the user through `auth.reauthenticate` and retry. With the [two-factor plugin](/auth/build/two-factor/) on and a factor confirmed, the request also needs a step-up held by the session or a code in `secondFactor`, or it answers `second_factor_required`. A new address that already has an account gets the same success answer and the same `expiresAt` as a free one, and its owner gets `email-change-in-use` instead of a code, so show "check the new address" either way. A new request replaces a pending one; a password change or reset, or signing out of other devices or everywhere, voids it. While the revert link of an earlier change is live, a new request answers `forbidden` (reason `email_change_pending_revert` in the audit row): tell the user they can change the address again once the link sent to their old address expires. Requests are limited per account (3 an hour) and per new address (3 an hour, from every account).

**Confirm.** The code is typed in a live signed-in session of the same account; in link mode (`emailChange.kind: 'link'`, with `urls.confirmEmailChange`) the link works only in such a session too, and is left unspent anywhere else, a revoked session included. On success the account moves to the new address, which is marked verified; every session of the account is revoked and the caller's is re-issued, so set the cookie of the session it returns. Reset and verification tokens mailed to the old address die, and the old address gets `email-changed` at once. If another account took the new address after the request, the answer is `email_in_use`; the confirmer has just proved that mailbox, so the answer tells them nothing about anyone else.

**Revert.** The old address's mail carries a link valid for 7 days (`emailChange.revertTtl`, which cannot be shorter). It needs no session. It moves the account back to the old address and removes the password in one write, then revokes every session, voids every reset, verification and pending change token, and runs the `onEmailReverted` hooks (the two-factor plugin removes a factor enrolled since the change). The next sign-in therefore fails until the user resets the password, and the reset goes to the restored address: tell them so on the page. The address the account lost is blocked for this account for 30 days (`emailChange.blockAfterRevert`), and the audit row `email.change_reverted` carries `review: true`. Route it to whoever looks at suspicious accounts.

If the old address has an account again (the hold narrows this to a race, or a direct store write), the revert answers `email_in_use` with reason `email_revert_address_taken`. It has still removed the password, revoked every session and pending token and run the hooks, and the `email.change_revert_failed` row carries `review: true` and `lockedOut: true`. The link is not spent: once support frees the address, the same link finishes the revert. Tell the user to contact support.

**What is not atomic.** Each flow is a series of store calls, not a transaction. Confirm writes the revert link and the hold before it moves the address, and revokes sessions after; a store error between leaves at worst an unmailed revert link for an address that did not move, which blocks nothing. Revert removes the password in the same write as the restore and revokes sessions right after; a store error after the restore leaves the link unspent, and clicking it again runs every step again.

## Answers

| Code | From | Show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fresh_auth_required` | request | the password prompt, then retry |
| `second_factor_required`, `invalid_second_factor` | request | the code prompt, then retry |
| `invalid_email` | request | "enter a valid address" (also for the account's current address) |
| `forbidden` | request | an earlier change can still be reverted, the address was blocked after a revert, or one of your hooks refused |
| `invalid_token` | confirm, revert | "the code or link is wrong or expired" |
| `email_in_use` | confirm, revert | the address was taken meanwhile |
| `session_expired` | any | sign in again |
| `rate_limited` | any | "try again later", with `retryAfterSeconds` |

## Options

| Option | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `emailChange.kind` | `'code'` | `'link'` needs `urls.confirmEmailChange`. |
| `emailChange.ttl` | `'15m'` for codes, `'1h'` for links | |
| `emailChange.digits` | `8` | 6 to 9. |
| `emailChange.maxAttempts` | `5` | Wrong guesses per code, counted before each comparison. |
| `emailChange.revertTtl` | `'7d'` | The minimum; a shorter value is refused at startup. |
| `emailChange.blockAfterRevert` | `'30d'` | |

Your own `beforeEmailChange` hook runs after the fresh-auth check and before anything is issued. It is given the normalised new address; refuse with a code that does not reveal whether that address is taken. An `onEmailReverted` hook gets the user id and `changedAt` after a revert (or a refused one) has locked the account out; it is awaited, and if it throws the revert fails with the link unspent.

## Limits

- **One change per revert window.** While a revert link is live the account cannot start another change, even when the user made the first one themselves. A typo the user noticed late waits for the link to expire, or for support.
- **An old address with an account anyway.** The hold keeps sign-up and other accounts' changes off the old address, but sign-up checks the hold before its insert, so a race can slip through, and a store written to directly ignores it. Then the revert locks the account out but cannot restore it, and the account still names the intruder's address until support frees the old one.
- **A factor from before the change stays.** The revert removes a factor enrolled since the change, but keeps an older one, so the owner's reset asks for it.
- **A new address's request limit can be spent by others.** `email-change-address` (3 an hour) counts requests to an address from every account, so anyone signed in who knows it can stall changes to it for an hour.
